title: Why Software Factories Fail
talk_summary: The speaker argues that lights-off software factories fail because models are RL-trained only on binary test-pass rewards, so they cannot be penalized for eroding maintainability, and no amount of harness/loop engineering fixes that. The remedy is to turn human review back on but make it cheap via AI-assisted upfront planning (product review, architecture, program design, vertical slices) so PRs are small, aligned, and fast to review.

takeaways.technique: Upfront planning artifacts before agent builds
takeaways.what_they_do: Before dispatching an agent, produce a product review (problem, desired behavior), architecture doc (component contracts, data models, constraints), program design (types, method signatures, call stacks), and vertical-slice implementation order with checkpoints.
takeaways.evidence_quote: 30 minutes over here in pre-planning and alignment can save you hours in review.
takeaways.numbers: 30 min planning vs hours of review (anecdotal)

takeaways.technique: Review small, aligned PRs instead of gating slop
takeaways.what_they_do: Keep human/agent review on, but shrink PR scope via planning so each PR is a joy to review; treat a drowning PR queue as a signal of too many bad PRs, not too few reviewers.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you don't have too many PRs. If you're drowning in PRs, you actually have too many bad PRs.

takeaways.technique: Penalize tests that don't fail pre-patch; judge code-quality rules
takeaways.what_they_do: Cites Frontier Code-style evals: penalize the model if its new tests pass on the pre-patch code (i.e., tests don't actually exercise the fix), plus a judge model checking adherence to code-quality rules.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if the model writes tests that don't fail on the pre-patch code, then it gets penalized.

takeaways.technique: Don't rely on model judges alone for maintainability
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues review agents and more tokens can raise the floor but are constrained by what RL taught; a model that knew good code would write it, so quality judging by models has a ceiling.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if the model knew what good code looks like, it would probably write it in the first place.

takeaways.what_they_do: Describes wiring monitoring/incidents and user feedback directly into the agent queue so fixes arrive as PRs rather than waking humans; the constraint becomes queue intake and review throughput.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You can take all the user feedback and just stick it straight into the factory so that people ask for stuff and it gets built.

takeaways.what_they_do: Plan implementation as ordered vertical slices across repos with explicit tests/checks between each phase, rather than one horizontal plan the model executes blindly.
takeaways.evidence_quote: vertical slices, which is the order of implementation, multi-repo coordination, how we're going to build this across our entire system, and how are we going to check it along the way.
